title: For the gurdwaras
hookLine: those who gave their lives to keep gurdwaras open and pure
last: THE MARTYRS — TO THE LAST BREATH.

lines: YOUR GURDWARA, AND YOU'RE NOT WELCOME.
THE DEEDS ARE IN HIS NAME.
cards: You walk to your gurdwara one morning, the place where your grandparents were married and your children were named, and the man who controls it tells you that people like you aren't welcome.
He treats the offerings as his own income. The deeds are in his name. The law, as it stands, is on his side.
What do you do? In the early 1920s, in Punjab, tens of thousands of Sikhs faced that question. Their answer cost many of them their lives, and the Ardas still remembers them in one short phrase.

teach.b: Among the ancient tortures in the martyrs' passage comes a phrase that sounds different: gurduaariaan dee sevaa laee kurbaaneeaan keeteeaan. Those who made sacrifices for the service of the gurdwaras.
The background: over the 1700s and 1800s, many historic gurdwaras came under hereditary custodians called mahants. Some cared for them faithfully.

Others came to treat the shrines as family property, and under British rule the courts often backed them. Some turned away Sikhs from so-called low castes, or allowed practices in the gurdwara that Sikh teaching rejects.
Between 1920 and 1925, Sikhs organized to take the gurdwaras back, in the Gurdwara Reform Movement. Its campaigns were called morchas, and many were deliberately nonviolent.
The worst day came in February 1921 at Nankana Sahib, Guru Nanak's birthplace. A peaceful group of Sikhs arrived to take over the shrine, and the mahant's armed men attacked them inside.
Well over a hundred were killed; sources differ on the number. At Guru ka Bagh in 1922, volunteers walked forward in batches to be beaten by police without raising a hand. The English clergyman C.
F. Andrews watched it happen and wrote about it, and reports like his carried the story far beyond Punjab.
In 1925 a new law placed the historic gurdwaras of Punjab under an elected Sikh committee, which still manages them.
So when Sikhs walk into a gurdwara today and find the doors open to everyone, the langar free, the Guru Granth Sahib honored, they're walking through doors that someone held open.
The Ardas asks them never to forget whose hands those were.

how: In every Ardas Sikhs remember those who sacrificed for the service of the gurdwaras, a line many connect with the Gurdwara Reform Movement of 1920 to 1925 and the Nankana Sahib massacre of 1921.

games.q: it's 1922 at Guru ka Bagh. police are beating each batch of Sikh volunteers who walk forward. you're in the next batch. what did the volunteers do?
o: walk forward without raising a hand.
games.why: they walked forward in batches and took the blows without striking back. C. F. Andrews, an English clergyman, watched and wrote about it.

practice: Picture a gurdwara, where anyone may enter, head covered and shoes off, and walk up to it in your mind: the shoe racks, the smell from the langar, the sound of kirtan.
Then picture the door itself, and the people who once stood there so that anyone could walk through it. If you pray, say Waheguru at the threshold.

wordCard.voice: Morcha, a nonviolent campaign: those who gave their lives in the 1920s so the gurdwaras would be open to all, and served as the Gurus taught.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: morcha, a front or campaign; the name for the reform movement's campaigns of the 1920s.

carryVoice: Your line: they kept the doors. Every open door was once held open by someone. That's day six hundred twenty-five.
